title: Postmortem: Elevated KV cache evictions increased costs and latency (2026-03-02)
author: Maya Srinivasan
content:
## Summary
On 2026-03-02 we observed a rise in KV cache evictions across the hosted fleet, leading to higher prefill compute, increased per-request latency, and higher unit cost.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 2 hours 12 minutes
- Symptoms: p95 latency +18% on long-context workloads; cost per 1k tokens +9%
- Scope: Hosted API, primarily long-context chat routes

## Detection
- Alert: cache eviction rate exceeded 5% on multiple clusters
- Cost dashboard: sudden increase in prefill FLOPs per token

## Timeline (UTC)
- 13:06: Eviction alert triggers
- 13:20: Runtime on-call confirms elevated evictions on A100 clusters
- 13:38: Mitigation: reduce max batch size for affected models; increase cache reservation
- 15:18: Evictions return to baseline

## Root cause
A batching policy change increased concurrent sequence lengths beyond the KV cache reservation assumptions for long-context workloads. The policy improved throughput on short prompts but caused memory pressure on mixed workloads.

## Contributing factors
- Mixed workload distribution not represented in canary
- Insufficient observability for "cache headroom" at the model instance level

## Follow-up action items
1. Add model-instance metric for KV cache headroom (reserved vs used) and alert on sustained <10% headroom. Owner team: Observability. Priority: P0.
2. Update batching policy to be workload-aware (cap concurrency when long-context requests dominate). Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
3. Add perf-canary scenario for mixed short/long workloads and verify eviction rate <1%. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
4. Add cost guardrail: alert when prefill FLOPs/token increases >7% week-over-week for a model route. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
5. Document safe batching configuration defaults by model family and GPU type in the serving runtime standards. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P2.

## Lessons learned
Throughput optimizations must be evaluated against mixed production distributions, not single-mode benchmarks. Cache headroom should be a first-class SLO for long-context serving.
